Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Patricia was sixty years old, a divorced state senator who had spent three decades in public life, and she had never imagined that a single moment could dismantle everything. It happened on a rainy November evening, two years ago, after a contentious town hall meeting. She had been driving herself home, still wired from the evening’s arguments, when her cell phone buzzed and she glanced down for an instant. That instant was enough. Her sedan drifted across the center line and clipped a motorcycle coming from the opposite direction. The rider—a twenty-eight-year-old father of two, she would later learn—was thrown onto the asphalt and sustained a traumatic brain injury. He survived, but he would never walk or speak the same way again. Patricia was not physically harmed, but something in her neck has ached ever since, a persistent, dull reminder that slots itself into her vertebrae whenever she feels any kind of pressure.

For months afterward, Patricia could not deliberately bring the crash to mind. She tried, in the early weeks, to reconstruct exactly what she had done—the moment of the lane drift, the wet pavement, the sound of metal folding—but the memory felt slippery and fragmented, like a locked drawer she could only peer at through a crack. But the images came back to her unbidden. She would be sitting in her office, and suddenly she would see—sharp and vivid—the front of her car slamming into the side of the motorcycle, the rider’s body lifting and spinning in the headlights before hitting the ground. The visual image was worse than the sound: the way the bike crumpled, how the man’s helmet smacked the asphalt. Once, during a committee hearing, a television in the corner of the room showed a news clip of a fender bender, and Patricia’s stomach lurched; she had to excuse herself to the restroom, where she stood gripping the sink and fighting the urge to retch. The same picture—a car hitting something, anything—could ambush her: a truck merging too closely, a parking lot fender bender, even a cartoon on a colleague’s coffee mug with a dented fender. She began avoiding any visual that might contain a collision, which meant she could not watch the evening news, could not scroll social media, could not walk past a television in a hotel lobby. The sounds came back too—the screech of tires, the hollow thud of impact, the silence afterward that was shattered by someone shouting “Oh my God, oh my God!” That shouting became a trigger even when it had nothing to do with the crash. During a committee hearing the next spring, a colleague raised his voice in frustration, and Patricia felt her throat close and her hands tremble. At first she did not connect it, but then the neck pain surged, and she knew. She started avoiding any situation where voices might rise—fundraisers, floor debates, even casual conversation in the hallway. She stopped attending caucus meetings. She told her staff she was delegating more.

Driving became impossible. She could not sit behind the wheel without her pulse hammering in her ears, and being a passenger was worse—she flinched at every lane shift, every approaching headlight, and the image of the crash would flash behind her eyes as if projected onto the windshield. She arranged for a driver, but even that felt like a surrender. She had always prided herself on independence, and now she had to schedule her days around a person who held the keys. The avoidance spread. She began to shut down any feeling, positive or negative, because all emotion felt dangerous—like a door that, once opened, might let the crash back in. She stopped laughing at jokes, stopped crying at funerals. She grew hollow and efficient. Her concentration frayed during briefings; she would read the same paragraph three times. Her staff noticed. Her colleagues noticed. At a press conference she froze mid-sentence because someone in the crowd had shouted a question, and she could not form a word for nearly a minute.

The humiliation was the part she could not shake. She had been a well-known name in the state, a woman who fought for road safety. And now she had caused the very thing she had campaigned against. She became convinced that everyone knew, that behind her back they said “there goes the woman who ruined a man’s life.” She blamed herself not only for the distracted glance but for every decision that led to that moment—taking the wheel when she was tired, not pulling over, not hiring a driver years ago. The guilt over her inaction was worse than the crash itself: she was certain she could have done more in the seconds before the impact—slammed the brakes, swerved harder, shouted a warning. She would never forgive herself.

What finally brought her to seek help was the near-collapse of her career. Her chief of staff had told her, gently, that she was going to lose the next primary if she could not attend debates. Patricia knew she could not step into a room where voices might rise, where a single shouted question could undo her. She was also terrified of the campaign trail itself: the inevitable television screens in hotel bars and airport terminals, the passing ambulances, any glimpse of a damaged car that might trigger the image of the motorcycle spinning in her headlights. She was afraid of being seen, afraid of letting anyone close, afraid that the memory would never loosen its grip. She came to the first session with her hands folded tightly in her lap, and she said, almost in a whisper, that she wanted to stop feeling so broken. She did not say she wanted to feel better; she said she wanted to stop being afraid of her own life—and of the pictures her own mind kept showing her.
